segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We are going to talk for a little while in Cherokee. That is what they want. The students might learn something from our conversation. And, also, for the Cherokee language to not fade away. They are fighting for this. But I don’t know what is going to happen to that. I am going to ask you this first—what is your name in English and in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Lula Elk, Geya.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, who named you that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It was Grandmother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Grandmother, oh yeah. They go back, where the elders lived and get names to give.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So it don’t fade away.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I think it was my grandpa’s mother’s name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born and what year was it you were born?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I was born at Hastings in Tahlequah. I am 63 years old. I live in Keys [Oklahoma] now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK yeah. Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Rocky Mountain.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was it like when you were growing up? For instance, were there lots of houses nearby or what?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No, my grandpa always had a garden.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That’s where I was working when I was growing up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were growing there. Or... What would you say?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were growing up there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can’t even talk.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like, for instance, children have things to play with. What did you have, when you were growing up, just something you made yourself?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yeah, I used to make bean flips.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were doing it like this [gestures]. You wasn’t hitting birds with a rock?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Or it was my brother.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You was probably hitting him with it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We used to make some like that—we used to try to hit birds with them. How old were you when you got a radio? Or when you all got one? Or say, for instance, a television?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I was about 12.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, so you were that old when you got a television?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they come to your house and watch it?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: One old man was going over there all the time on Saturday to watch wrestling.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, wrestling.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I didn’t like that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I didn’t either. But Dad and Grandma were watching it all the time—that wrestling. They would go to Fort Smith and watch them. I would go. I would be crying. When they started fighting I would be scared.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Ha ha.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They really liked it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that oldest boy at the house, he always used to want to go to wrestling. One day they came to where I’m from. He was begging us. So we got frustrated with him and gave him the money. And he went [to see wrestling]. When he got back, after they got done, he said, “Mom?” She said, “What?” He said “That’s fake, it’s not true.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s true. Boy, I was still afraid. I didn’t like it—hitting each and doing that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess it’s different now, where you grew up, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It is, does your mind sometimes go back to where you grew up? And think “This is the way it was back then.” Does it come to you like that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, all the time. It seems that’s what happens to me. I go to the stomp ground, it is there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah. “This is the way it was, back then,” you think when you think about it. I guess it’s really changed there now.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It has.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is the best thing you remember growing up, when you think about it? Like for instance, did you climb trees or just different things?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Just different things. I used to go to the stomp grounds all the time. That seems to be what I know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So, you liked to do that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you were growing up, like for instance, your grandmother or your relatives—did they live close by?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Some did. Two of my uncles lived in Tulsa, and the others were just there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just there. They just lived near where you grew up. So, you were living good? Y’all helped each other, no doubt.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yeah, it was good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, it’s good when it’s like that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How many of you children were there?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Me? Seven.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Seven. I don’t know why I was thinking just two. Are you the oldest?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Loretta—Tommy passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, I didn’t know. She went to school with Darrel. His friend, sometimes he talks about her. He remembers her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I went to Zion school, near Stilwell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you first started, did you already know how to speak English a little bit?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I didn’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you had a rough time?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, those kids were always doing something. I was sitting there, and didn’t know what the teacher was saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was really hard, ain’t it? If you didn’t understand.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they tell Getsisgage not to speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They didn’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They didn’t?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would really ( sgasdi) ( tsigogisgagv) tell us not to be speaking in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That one teacher was telling me, “When you get to your house speak in all English.” There wasn’t anyone that spoke in English. At my house we all were making sounds all in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: We were the same way.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The same—all of you and your siblings spoke in all Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As time went on, one teacher told me, “Don’t ever lose your Cherokee speaking.” Yeah. Where all have you worked, when you were growing up and became an adult?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Stilwell Foods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Stilwell Foods, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: All the people worked there, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we have talked to a lot that have worked there at Stilwell Foods. And, also, what is that called, where they raise flowers?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Greenleaf?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s Greenleaf.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How long did you work there?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Stilwell Foods, it was about four years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. There were probably a lot of Cherokees working at Stilwell Foods.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all fit in together, and y’all were talking in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: There was a lot of Mexicans working there, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They were working there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you get along with them?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I guess so. I didn’t say anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So you just stayed quiet. I guess it’s better to do that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like, for instance, are you a musician for instance? Or, guitar or piano—you ever messed with anything like that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, can you sing?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Maybe.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Can you sing us one?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I don’t know any.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you hear, you probably remember, then you follow them.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I dance at the stomp grounds.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How about when you finished Zion, where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: To Tulsa—that is where my dad lived.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So you finished there?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You didn’t?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I quit.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was it hard going to school out that way, Tulsa? There must’ve been a lot of children?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There probably wasn’t any Cherokees going to school there. Or, were there some there?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Some of those Drywaters were going to school there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Drywaters. Which Drywaters were those?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Like Becky, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I think so, and that Jerry Drywater.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Jerry Drywater.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: He lived in Lyon Switch, that-One.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, do you remember if there were any by the name Cochran, going to school there?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: My mom was Dorthy Wolfe.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dorthy Wolfe.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: My dad was Bowdark Charles Elk.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Charles Elk, yeah. Did they live around where you grew up?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I think my mom was born in Fort Gibson. And Dad, I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: My grandmother and grandfather’s name was Wolfe—Jim and Margie Wolfe.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that was your grandma and grandpa.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you visit them all the time?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That is where I lived.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, they raised you?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, that’s it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is good, ain’t it, to go there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many... You got any children?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, there is just three now—two boys and the girl.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they speak Cherokee growing up?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They were trying, that-One had a fatal accident—Smokey Mankiller, that-One.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was Uton’s friend, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You do know he passed, too—Uton?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, Uton.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like, for instance, your grandma and grandpa, did they know any medicine from the woods, like roots?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they know a lot?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: A lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you learn?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: A little bit, not all of it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It was a lot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You’re not paying attention when you are a child, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: You don’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s like that for me. I think, nowadays, I should have listened. They knew a lot of medicine from the woods back then—the roots.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I am still learning.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. I guess that is all we had to help us, is what our grandparents and parents knew. What medicine to get from the woods. When I was growing up there wasn’t hardly any doctors nearby. So, we used mostly things like that—’root medicine’—and that would get us across when we were sick. Some of it, I really didn’t like it— was too strong. “Drink it. It’s medicine. It is going to help you,” they would tell me.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, that is better.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Those pills ain’t good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess there is nobody that does that now—medicine.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My sister’s husband’s grandmother knew extremely a lot. She would have taught me if I wanted to. But I was too much of a young boy, then. I did not want to learn anything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It would have been good if I would have listened, I think now. When they talk about—she was around 140 years old when she passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ooh…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She really knew a lot of medicine.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t think my grandparents knew anything. All I remember is I used to always get boils. My grandpa said, “I am going to teach you how to heal yourself.” He said, “I am only going to tell you one time, and if you don’t learn it...” I did learn that. I guess that’s all he knew. I don’t know if he knew anything else. I don’t think he knew anything else.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But, some that know medicine like that, they have been chosen they say.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is true, that’s what I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wasn’t chosen, I don’t think.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But if it’s a man he has to teach a woman, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And [if it’s] a woman [she must teach] a man—that’s what I heard. I learned that, ‘cause I used to get boils all the time.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That one medicine—I forget what the name is in Cherokee—but, in English it’s calamus. When Covid was going around, I went and got that and I told all those children to eat it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They didn’t catch Covid?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Are you saying ‘calamus’?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where can you find that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: At a pond—it is like cattails, but it is not cattail. [cattail, bulrush, Typha spp.]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But it looks the same as that? How can you tell that is what it is, that it’s not that [cattails, bulrush]?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That is really strong that root.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s good if you know that. They say that [Covid] is coming back again. Me and my wife made it through. I don’t know about that. We didn’t use anything—we believe God got us through. Do you remember, growing up, they say, “Gadugi, teamwork.” They used to say, if someone was sick, they would go and help them out. Or if someone passed away, back then, they would have a wake, service, for the one that passed. But they don’t do that now. Do you remember that? Did y’all go—if they were doing that somewhere?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I do that, when that-Boy passed away—he was laying at the house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He spent the night.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yeah, at nighttime.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, they used to say, “They are going to make a last stop at their house,” they used to say.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They don’t hardly do that anymore, do they?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No. When my husband passed it was the same. But my cousin fixed the casket.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He made it? They will let you do that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They will let you.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They did not do anything at the funeral—just embalm him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I think they have laws to do that—embalm.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I think they said, “It is 72 hours.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I had just finished school; I was going toward town. I got along with the funeral-home workers. I was walking, they called my name, and said my name, and said, “Come here.” So I went that way. “You want to work?” they said. I said, “No.” I said, “Doing what?” They said “Sitting by the desk, answering the phone.” I said “Is that all?” “That is all you have to do.” I said, OK. So I started. One time, late night, that-Police’s son was knocking. He was saying, “Get up, Guy.” I was thinking, “Who is knocking again?” It was that-Police. I said, “What do you want?” He said, “Get up we have to pick up a dead body.” Gah-lee, it was late at night, too. I said, “I am not supposed to be doing that.” He said, “Yes, you are. That is what my dad said.” His dad was [in] the police. He said, “Get, let’s go.” Gosh. We went to get that one-that-passed-away, late at night. Boy, it was scaring me. And that White man wasn’t thinking nothing. He was used to that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It doesn’t seem like you would ever get used to it, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, really. I just worked there for a little while. That last time I had enough, so I quit. Did your parents ever talk about where the Cherokees come from—old Cherokee, they say? They may have heard something somewhere.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: My grandpa used to say there were Cherokees living in New York. That is why those men, when they saw those white boats, were saying, “Run, run.” And when those White people heard that, or Cherokees, he said—that is why it is in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes some talk about when they left—old Cherokee. Some talk about how they would be walking somewhere, and they would hide. And that is why there are still some living there, they say.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That is what they were saying—they hid.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I went to Tennessee, one time, to preach. And I asked if there were any Cherokees there. They said there was some, living in the northern and eastern part of Tennessee. But I never did see them. And, also, there were Cherokees in Georgia. They said, when they were coming, they got off somewhere and they hid. Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you think about it, they came through some bad times, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they absolutely did. Y’all planted a garden when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all have a huge garden?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: We really did.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you all can?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, corn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Corn.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Beans and tomatoes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee, and also potatoes?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Potatoes. I was sitting in the middle of those tomatoes, holding salt.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were eating them [with salt]. You were eating up what was planted in the garden. Did you just quit working at Stilwell Foods?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where did you start then?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Nowhere.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You just took a break for a little while?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Didn’t you work here for a while? [Cherokee Nation]

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: For how long, here?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I started here in 2001, and I retired in 2019.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did you do at Cherokee Nation?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I was a teacher.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I was going to South Coffeyville.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You was going all the way over there, to teach Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It was everything, and they were making baskets.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where is Coffeyville?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Kansas, towards the north. When you get out of Oklahoma, Coffeyville is close by.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they want to, or were you teaching White people? Or, are there Cherokees living out that way?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They are a little bit Cherokee there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were part.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Some also lived in Bartlesville and went to South Coffeyville.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Were you teaching there at nighttime?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: -- Also, one time, where was it...? I had to go that way. I got to know some Cherokees. They were doing good, living there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess there are Cherokees living everywhere, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I mean—Florida, everywhere, and different states. I wonder what it would be like, I think. If you could go there and talk about teaching Cherokee. What would they do? I wonder if they would want to, come to think about it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They might be OK with it.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I think about it. I don’t know how many are living in those places.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They probably would want to learn.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: To learn? I am going to go there. Not really.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: To Florida.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Get in a bus. For instance, did you all look for things, sometimes, from the woods—like blueberry or wild onion and...?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Polk salad and, they called ‘kotsunegi’—‘long time ago.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I have never ate it. Is it good?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was good.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: It’s good, and polk salad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yesterday a woman came, you know. No, it was Monday. She was telling us—if you just buy a can of spinach... Was it you?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, I was by myself. I was by myself. “If you just buy a can of spinach, and cook it, and put eggs in it,” she said. I did that last night.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it good?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I spent the night at Dad’s. I told him “Let’s try. And so I cooked it, and put three eggs in it. I used two cans.” It turned out good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many eggs did you put in there?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Three.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Three.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Three, I mixed with two cans [of spinach].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you warm that spinach in a skillet?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, I poured a little oil in there. I cooked that for a little while. I cooked it for about ten minutes, then put three eggs in there. It turned out good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dad said, “It’s real good.” He almost ate it up. I said, “Wait, I want a little bit.” That’s what she said, her grandmother used to do that. It was really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I am going to tell my wife to do that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You don’t have to go look for it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He also likes hot-water cornbread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He said make that, too. So then I made that, too.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He ate good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, and he also likes macaroni.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Macaroni and cheese?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just macaroni.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: With just a little oil poured in. He puts pepper and salt.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then I made him that. It was about ten, he was eating.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: He was hungry.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was saying, “This is good.” He really ate that. Have you ever ate that? Boil the macaroni, when it’s done then pour a little oil and salt, that’s it.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I eat rice like that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Like that.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: And salt and pepper, and a little oil—it good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I am going to try that, too. I’m hungry now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If someone says they are Cherokee. Or, they say, “I am Cherokee.” What comes to your mind? If someone says they are Cherokee.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Gateyo—stompground dancing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What comes to your mind, when someone says they are Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Just that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it how we speak? We can make an example using our hands, and say it was this big [gestures]. When I went fishing I caught a fish this big [gestures]. And a White man will not hardly use his hands.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And also, for instance, if someone stumps their toe and falls down us Cherokees will start laughing at them.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We will view it even funnier. That is what I tell my husband when we talk about something and we laugh. I tell him, “They ain’t no reason me telling you, cause it’s not funny in English.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For instance, if it’s a White man, he will say “Are you alright?” And help them up. And us Cherokees will laugh at them, for instance. “Does it hurt?” We will say. They will say, “It hurts!” They say, “Would... You would hurt, too, if you fell down.” And just be funny.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Or you would be laughing at yourself, if something happened to you.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: If I fall down, the kids will do the same thing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, also, y’all have probably done this, if you stump your toe and you almost fall down, you look around. Y’all have done that. A Cherokee will do that, ain’t it. And say, “I wonder who seen me.” Really. When us Cherokees talk about something, we will use our hands and faces. We will say, “Where was it at?” And then we will say, “It was over there,” with our faces.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was over there! I do that all the time. The boys will say, “Why do you do that all the time?” “I’m just used to it,” I tell them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If it’s a Cherokee, they are going to do that, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, also, if he thinks it’s strange, they will say, “Is that it?” And a white man will say, “Oh, is that right?”

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Or they will say, “It really is.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it, that’s why we are Cherokees. That’s what I think about how we Cherokees will be laughing. One elder said, ‘long time ago, “It don’t matter how much debt a Cherokee has, they will just be laughing.” And a White man will be thinking about it. He will be thinking about his debt. And a Cherokee will be laughing around, he said. It really is like that, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We mean it when we talk, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There is a difference. “That is the way we Cherokees are,” that elder said. And when I thought about it good—that is the way we Cherokees are, I thought. Your parents, your grandmother, did she talk about anything interesting? For instance, I ask them, like, little people—if they have seen, or if they have heard, little people? Or, did they hear anything like that, or told you?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: “Don’t talk about them,” they said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, really? Yeah. Did they hear them talking or what?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No, they didn’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about seeing a tsigili, did they talk about anything like that?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That one time, at night. It looked like a fire this big [gestures]. It took off, flying by my house, and it scared me. And my grandfather said it was a kolen.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess those were really mean.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they are bad. They are the baddest ones, they say, ‘long time ago.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: That is what Grandpa was saying. I said, “What is a kolen?”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember one time my dad called. He said, “Y’all come over here, right now.” I said, “Why?” “I was feeding hogs, and a big fire went into y’alls’ house,” he said. I thought, “What could it be?” So, I left from there, quickly. “Yes,” he said, “It went in there.” He said he was feeding cows, horses, and it flew by. He said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. When someone is sick they would see one like that. They would say, one-like-that flew over there. They say, “It is looking for something, to help itself.” One time, where I’m from, there was a hospital. A friend of mine was telling me, or was talking about it. They took their grandmother to the doctor at the hospital. They sat her down. And, after a while, the doctor looked at him, and was doing this [gestures]. He was thinking, “What is it?” He said, in English, “This old woman, setting right here, don’t even have a little bit of blood in her body.” It was empty. That old lady was sitting close. That’s what kind she was—a kolen. He said that doctor told him, she should have been gone ‘long time ago. She didn’t have any blood inside of her.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It scared me even more, he said, but.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You have seen little people?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Are some friendly, or some mean, or what?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes they were friendly—they were laughing all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes. I used to go behind my house all the time. There was a pool of water there. Here there was, like, steps on the rocks, and they were there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Were they little, just this tall [gestures]?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They are little.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They weren’t afraid of you? They didn’t see you? Or did they see you?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, and they were not afraid of you?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about you? You wasn’t afraid of them?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: No, I wasn’t. Because they were good. At first—they were afraid, and I was afraid.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There was a friend of mine, from towards where I am from. They lived by the water. In the summertime, he used to go swimming. One time, he said, he was swimming. ‘Seen some, little people were sitting by a bluff. He said they were just ye tall [gestures]. I said, “Did they see you?” He said, “Yes, they seen. But they were swimming, too. They were diving in the water. They were talking, too. And I was doing the same thing. But they didn’t do anything to me,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I wonder why, it seems when people talk about seeing them, it is by the water?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. He was telling me he sees them all the time. I don’t know if it’s true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They didn’t want to play, or what... Were they just hanging around there?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: They were just hanging around there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They say they will get you lost.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, but it didn’t seem like they wanted to.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. Some talk about seeing them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: One man talked about how they healed him. He was sick—you remember that Guy? He said he was laying down sick, or... It was Charlie. Those little people came in, and healed him, he said. That was all they did. Then they left, he said. I don’t know if I want to see one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You would not want to be healed?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I would like to be healed. But I don’t know if I want to see them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That really is interesting, things like that. I am going to ask you this now. You don’t read in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, you can read?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be was it easy for you to learn.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes, it was OK. I used to read those thick books.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For me, one time there was a preacher from where I come from. He was going around, teaching Cherokee. And I would go with him, and ride with him. He would say, “Are we going?”—I could learn what he was teaching. Then, one day, I told my wife. She said, “Read the Bible, in the front it is written—like you said. Just read those.” Then I did that for a few days. Then, one time, I think it was a preacher that was telling me, “If you try to read the book of John, that is easy to learn to read.” He said, “John, the good news.” So when I started it was getting easy to read the book of John. He said, “That is the easiest to read.” And it was then, as time went on, I would get to a different place. At a slow pace, I was learning.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You taught yourself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Boy, when I first started learning, it was hard for me. I finally learned.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me too, I had a rough time. Some talk about back then they had a dream. Then the next day they were able to read Cherokee. I would wonder why I couldn’t have a dream. I thought, “Gaw.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about, as time goes on, do you think Cherokee will fade away? Or, do you think it will keep going, just like it is, say, for instance in 20 years?

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: I think it will get stronger.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: What they are doing here—they are teaching good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It will be joyful if that happens.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: There is a lot of people that want to learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: True, true. As well as the White people.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes. That boy, my son Smokey, we were at Long John Silver at lunch time. Mary Cochran, also. And Smokey was sitting there, listening. We were talking Cherokee, and laughing. And Smokey said, “Mom.” I said, “What?” He said, “I want to learn Cherokee. I want to laugh at people, and they won’t know what I’m talking about.” I said, “Smokey, we don’t do that.” He said, “You are always laughing.” I said, “Yes.” It was funny.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I’m from, the storekeepers I say, “Wado” [thank you]. I teach them a little bit. I say, “Wado.” They say, “Howa’ the White people?” “They are learning from me talking to them,” I say. “Are you OK?” Boy, they say good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They are understanding.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They understand a little bit. Well, I am glad we had this conversation. We talked in all Cherokee.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s joyful to find someone that talks in Cherokee, and is Cherokee, so you can talk in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: lula-elk
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m glad I got to know you for a little while.
